data.title: Is it lights out for Singapore’s night-time economy?
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore does well in attracting visitors for major events, from Formula 1 and concerts to conferences and exhibitions.

Liu Dongjie, who is pursuing a Master of Business Administration at Nanyang Technological University (NTU), recounts that pop star Taylor Swift’s six sold-out shows in 2024 were a “trigger” for his overseas friends to visit the city-state.

But when they went to Clarke Quay – Singapore’s iconic riverside nightlife enclave – after the concert, most restaurants were already closed. The group found the late-night options limited.

“They just came for the event,” he says. “There is no retention for Singapore.”

By all accounts, the Republic’s nightlife sector has turned moribund.

The operating revenue of pubs, nightclubs, discotheques, dance clubs and karaoke lounges fell by more than half in the last decade, from S$674.7 million in 2015 to S$284.7 million in 2022, based on a white paper released by the Singapore Nighttime Business Association (SNBA) in September this year.

The night-time economy “is struggling, if I’ll be honest”, says SNBA president Danny Loong. “I think we are trying to adjust to the new realities.”

No place like home

Singapore’s nights used to be livelier. From the 1980s to the 2000s, nightclubs and supper spots kept people out well past midnight. But the city’s club scene has since thinned.

The iconic Zouk remains, albeit at a different location, but several other well-known venues – such as The Butter Factory, St James Power Station and Shanghai Dolly – have closed down.

Most malls close by 10 pm, limiting after-work shopping options, while drinking establishments must stop serving alcohol before midnight.

At the same time, any night-time buzz needs people who are willing to head out.

Liu and his classmates learnt from interviews with NTU students that some prefer gathering in their dormitories – where they can drink more cheaply, play their own music, and avoid the transport costs of getting home after public buses and trains have stopped operating.

Businesses are “competing with a behavioural default of staying at home”, notes Dr Tan Kim Lim, head of James Cook University Singapore’s Centre for International Trade and Business in Asia.

He adds that the Covid-19 pandemic reinforced this habit, while digital technology makes at-home entertainment options more attractive and convenient.

Another hurdle that SNBA identified is the expense of getting home after a night out. The consumer price index for point-to-point transport services was 45 per cent higher in September 2026 than in September 2021.

This increased cost adds to the price of an after-dark jaunt – making it less appealing to some to head out late.

Rethinking nightlife

One bright spot is that dining out remains popular with Singapore residents. In a 2025 Knight Frank-Ipsos survey, 66 per cent of local respondents selected dining as a preferred leisure activity, compared with 10 per cent who chose clubbing and nightlife. 

The F&B industry is thus a stalwart propping up late-night pastimes. But more eateries may not be enough to sustain the sector.

Kent Teo, CEO of events firm Invade, describes F&B as a “super red ocean” – a loss-making segment, with home-grown businesses struggling to compete in a market saturated with foreign brands.

For Loong, the solution is not simply to bring back clubs and bars. “These days, it’s about building experience, placemaking, place management and combining all these different parts together to make it more vibrant,” he says.

That broader remit is reflected in SNBA’s recent rebrand – until August, it was called the Singapore Nightlife Business Association – and its recommendations.

Against this backdrop, SNBA’s precinct approach aims to draw people out by bringing local businesses, cultural activities and public spaces together.

Lewis Lim, associate professor of marketing practice at NTU’s Nanyang Business School, supervised Liu and several other MBA students on a project conducted in collaboration with SNBA.

Informed in part by the students’ research, the SNBA white paper proposes broadening the night economy beyond bars and clubs to include shopping, creative industries and cultural activities, among others.

It also calls for better late-night transport, a “night pass” offering credits for transport and ticketed experiences, a national night-time economy office, as well as distinctive precincts including Holland Village, Clarke Quay, Orchard Road and Kampong Glam.

These proposals would complement other efforts to enliven Singapore’s precincts after dark.

In August, the government formalised such measures trialled for a year in Boat Quay, Clarke Quay and Upper Circular Road, including later alcohol trading hours and the resumption of Circular Road closures for events. 

The Singapore Tourism Board’s Orchard Road Rejuvenation Initiative, which was unveiled in May, similarly supports industry-led night programming, including curated markets and extended operating hours tied to events.

Loong, the SNBA president, thinks transport and precinct development are among the proposals that can realistically be pursued. Talks with the authorities on transport are under way, he says, declining to elaborate beyond describing them as “constructive”.

Precincts as multipliers

The precinct proposal is central to SNBA’s case that Singapore can compete for the night-time dollar on unique offerings rather than price.

Home-grown brands and creative talent, the white paper says, can become “destination assets” that help define what experiencing Singapore after dark means.

The organisation argues that neighbourhoods should be places for Singaporeans to enjoy and identify with, which will draw visitors seeking to experience what locals do.

According to the white paper, successful precincts need strong identities, which can be built through coordinated programming, attractive public spaces, cultural activity and collaboration among government, communities and businesses.

That identity would come from a mix of local restaurants, bars, cafes, entertainment concepts, music venues, cultural businesses, retailers and lifestyle operators.

The NTU researchers describe what that mix should offer visitors: places to eat, listen to music and stay late, alongside hotels, transport and safe waiting spaces. 

A walkable precinct would let people move between them without taking a private-hire ride to continue their night elsewhere, easing some concerns about transport costs.

This mix can also make it less risky for businesses to extend their hours.

NTU’s Prof Lim says one operator may hesitate to stay open late alone, but if nearby businesses do the same, their combined offerings can give people more reason to visit.

“There’s an ecosystem there. One kind of business makes another more attractive. It’s a multiplier effect.”

Home-grown businesses can anchor precincts with offerings and experiences that overseas visitors are less likely to find in their home countries, notes Musa Fazal, chief policy and operating officer of the Singapore Business Federation (SBF).

Supporting local businesses

SNBA’s Loong also hopes landlords will consider the tenant mix.

“Everybody plays a part in building up our culture and creating space for something more uniquely Singapore,” he says. “If we are going to be uniquely Singapore, then we have to have Singapore brands.”

But these may struggle in a crowded real estate market where foreign brands, such as restaurant chains from mainland China, can pay record rents and crowd out smaller players.

Noting that “shopping malls have become ‘copy-and-paste’, because whoever can pay stays”, Invade’s Teo suggests building lifestyle destinations out of empty school compounds in the Singapore Land Authority’s land bank.

For instance, the former Nan Chiau High School campus at Kim Yam Road has been reinvented as New Bahru, which houses home-grown food, retail, art, wellness and design brands. Evening offerings include a coffee-shop-cum-taproom, cultural gatherings and live performances.

Similarly, Hong Kong’s PMQ is a former police housing complex turned creative hub, while Taipei’s Songshan Cultural and Creative Park used to be a tobacco factory.

Even so, Teo acknowledges that such spaces lack malls’ ready-made amenities, meaning that operators would have to invest in facilities and renovations.

On top of that, rents would need to be effectively subsidised to offset those costs – and that still does not guarantee the spaces would draw a night-time crowd.

“If people are not even coming out, then we don’t need to talk about rental at all,” he says.

Therefore, he also calls for efforts to improve existing businesses, such as Clarke Quay’s eateries and live performance venues, which are “not exactly doing too well”.

“If we want to focus on the night-time economy, we need to focus on what is already here,” he says.

Prof Lim adds that government support may also be needed to “help some sectors for the greater good”, especially in enabling small businesses to become more established.

Uphill effort

In August, SNBA partnered government agency Enterprise Singapore, merchants and other stakeholders to test its pitch for distinctive night-time precincts in the expat enclave of Holland Village. 

Teo from Invade put on a festival dubbed Village Encounters, which ran for a weekend from 4 to 10 pm. The event featured games, workshops and family activities, with DJs and roving street acts and other performances later in the evening.

Seeing dining and live music as ways to build on Holland Village’s neighbourhood character, SNBA plans to work with partners on at least four more projects to develop selected precincts over the next two years.

Teo says the event recorded 26,265 visits – that is 2.6 to 5.3 times the usual traffic of 5,000 to 10,000 visits on a normal weekend, based on his team’s estimate.

Village Encounters also drew people beyond Holland Village’s regular visitors. Invade’s post-event survey of attendees shows that 45.8 per cent said it was their first visit to the enclave, or that they had visited only once or twice in the past year.

More than half said they had spent over S$20 at local F&B or retail businesses. And while 91.9 per cent of the 208 respondents said they would probably or definitely return to Holland Village within three months, actual return visits were not tracked.

Business owners tell The Business Times that results have been mixed.

Despite not participating in Village Encounters, pet store Fur saw its sales rise during the festival weekend. But Donald Kng, co-founder and CEO of parent company Vetreska, remarks that he cannot link the increase to the event.

Olivier Dyens, owner of Italian restaurant La Nonna, estimates that sales rose 15 to 20 per cent during the event, with till takings covering promotional voucher redemptions.

Yet, Wala Wala Cafe Bar owner Stanley Yeo describes the sales impact at his well-known establishment as marginal, even though some visitors who came for complimentary mocktails also ordered food.

Still, he takes a longer view of the event crowd. “There is value in simply getting people back into Holland Village.”

He adds: “They may not necessarily come into Wala Wala that particular weekend, but seeing the area and the businesses here can remind them that we are still around and give them a reason to return another time.”

Loong calls the event “just a starting point” – a showcase that supports SNBA’s plans to develop more night-time precincts in 2027.

He acknowledges that getting malls, shophouse businesses, retailers, eateries and entertainment venues to work together will take time, but he believes that regular events can give them more opportunities to do so.

Bottoms up

Reviving Singapore’s nightlife is a challenge with high stakes.

Beyond the fate of individual night-time establishments, quieter nights can be a drag on the broader economy, notes NTU’s Prof Lim. He says Singapore is missing out – for now – on an opportunity to encourage longer stays and capture more visitor spending.

Visitors stayed for an average of 3.48 days in 2025, based on Singapore Tourism Board data. If that is roughly three nights, Prof Lim estimates that one more night would extend the average stay by about a third, potentially bringing in significantly more tourism receipts.

“There’s a lot of money that can be earned,” he says, especially since daytime attractions offer little for business travellers who spend sunlit hours at conferences or exhibitions.

At the same time, the Singapore dollar goes further across the border, and Johor Bahru can tempt Singaporean night owls with a plethora of late-night activities – from affordable massages to go-karting – that are harder to come by in the Republic.

The opening of the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link in 2027 adds to the pressure. An SBF study estimates that the new cross-border connection could lead to a net S$290 million increase in annual spending flowing out of Singapore and across the Causeway.

SBF’s Musa tells BT that preparations to deal with the heightened competition should begin early, particularly where businesses need time to adjust.

“The objective is not to prevent cross-border spending – greater connectivity will naturally give consumers more choice,” he says. “It is to ensure Singapore businesses can compete on their strengths and capture opportunities in a larger, more integrated market.”

On the home front, Loong points to the recent formation of an alliance co-chaired by SNBA and SBF that brings together trade associations for the restaurant, hotel and retail industries.

“We cannot work in silos anymore,” says Loong. “You’ve got to have everybody in.”

data.title: China’s Cabinet stresses market support in rare statement; vows more moves to stabilise stocks
data.description:
CHINA’S State Council reaffirmed its support for the capital market in a rare midday readout of its meeting, emphasising the role of the so-called national team and pledging to roll out more policies to stabilise equities.

Beijing will improve policies guiding long-term funds into stocks and encourage listed companies to step up dividend payouts and share buybacks, according to the Xinhua News Agency. 

The statement comes at a precarious time for Chinese stocks, with most equity benchmarks entrenched in a bear market amid tepid earnings and a weak economy.

The CSI 300 Index has lost 16 per cent so far in 2026, putting it on track for its worst year since 2022.

While authorities sought to revive investor confidence through a slew of measures in October and state funds have been actively buying, they have mostly been seen as stemming the bleeding rather than engineering a recovery. 

“The statement shows that stabilising the capital market remains a priority at the highest levels of government, which should help ease negative sentiment,” said Fu Zhifeng, chief investment officer at Shanghai Chengzhou Investment Management.

“After the recent sell-off, investors have shown little appetite to buy the dip, while much of the selling pressure may have already been exhausted. The announcement can therefore provide further support to the market this afternoon.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Malaysia, Singapore can win bigger deals together: Economy Minister Akmal
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Malaysia and Singapore can win investments that neither could attract as effectively on its own by helping companies operate across the border, Malaysia’s Economy Minister Akmal Nasir said. This comes as businesses reassess where to expand amid rising trade uncertainty.

He pointed to the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) as a way for companies to run complementary operations on both sides of the border.

Covering 3,588 square km across Iskandar Malaysia and Pengerang, JS-SEZ is a cross-border economic initiative that pairs Singapore’s capital, connectivity and global business links with Johor’s land, industrial base and lower operating costs.

Formalised on Jan 7, 2025, the zone also aims to make it easier to move workers, goods and capital across the border, and to reduce the regulatory and administrative hurdles of operating in two countries.

“The test of this partnership is about the delivery,” Akmal said on Friday (Nov 27), pointing to early investment figures as a measure of how the two countries were turning cooperation into projects.

Akmal was delivering a keynote speech at SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit 2026, jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

The annual event gathered policymakers, business leaders and industry experts, with OCBC as the presenting sponsor, Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

The Malaysian and Singaporean governments are also working on a blueprint that will serve as the joint operational road map for both countries in translating the earlier framework agreement into concrete policies, agency workflows and infrastructure timelines.

They initially aimed at launching the blueprint next week, but it has been deferred to early 2027, according to Akmal in an interview with ST, as both governments need more time to finalise the details to ensure a smooth roll-out.

He also mentioned that a special pass for workers commuting across the border could be finalised as part of the blueprint.

More than half of approved investment implemented

JS-SEZ recorded RM88.8 billion (US$21.6 billion) in approved investments between January 2025 and June 2026, of which about RM40.3 billion, or nearly 62 per cent, had been implemented.

The figures, first disclosed by a bilateral ministerial committee on Nov 2, showed that the approved projects could create 28,755 jobs. Projects already implemented accounted for 12,796 of those jobs.

Akmal said for Singapore, the zone gives businesses room to expand and diversify their supply chains, while for Malaysia, it is a way to attract higher-value investment, bring more local firms into supply chains and give workers opportunities to develop technical skills.

The investment pitch comes as companies weigh how tariffs affect their access to customers, how geopolitical tensions could disrupt shipping routes and energy supplies, and how much it will cost to power new operations.

Akmal noted that these pressures can compound one another, giving economies with dependable infrastructure and trade links an advantage when businesses decide where to expand.

Malaysia’s focus

For Malaysia, Akmal noted that the current focus is on four areas under the 13th Malaysia Plan: high-value industries and advanced manufacturing; semiconductor design and advanced packaging; artificial intelligence adoption and digital transformation; and clean energy and green industries.

As the plan enters its second year in 2027, he said the country aims to sustain momentum by making local participation, technology transfer and skills development integral to investment.

“Success will be measured by stronger local suppliers, higher productivity and better jobs. The partnership with Singapore is an early example of this approach,” he added.

Malaysia’s economy expanded 5.6 per cent in the first nine months of 2026, supported by domestic demand and the external sector. Unemployment stood at 3 per cent in the third quarter.

Akmal expects full-year economic growth to exceed 5 per cent, aligned with an earlier forecast by Malaysia’s central bank.

Time to diversify supply chains

He pointed out that Asia’s faster growth gave it time to diversify supply chains and invest in skills and technology before the next shock.

The International Monetary Fund’s October outlook projected that emerging and developing Asia would grow 5.1 per cent in 2026 and the Asean-5 by 4.4 per cent, both above its global forecast of 3.1 per cent.

He urged Asian economies to keep trade and investment open as companies diversify their supply chains.

The Johor-Singapore partnership showed how neighbours could use their different strengths to draw investment and widen opportunities for businesses and workers on both sides of a border, he added.

“Our future cannot be shaped in isolation… We cannot work in silos,” said Akmal.

data.title: Data centres to double Malaysian electricity demand by 2050
data.description:
MALAYSIAN electricity demand is set to more than double through 2050 due to a rapid buildout of power-hungry data centres.

Energy needs will rise to 49.8 gigawatts by mid-century from 22.5 gigawatts in 2027, the Ministry of Energy Transition and Water Transformation said on Thursday (Nov 26).

Data centres will account for 21 per cent of power demand by 2050, up from 11 per cent in 2027, the ministry said.

The South-east Asian nation has ambitious plans to be a regional hub for artificial intelligence.

It’s drawn billions of dollars of investment from tech heavyweights including Oracle, Amazon.com and Alphabet’s Google, which plans to spend US$15 billion to expand data centre and cloud operations in Malaysia over the next two years. 

Tighter US restrictions on access to technology could hinder Malaysia’s plan, however.

Concerns that Nvidia chips are being smuggled to China via South-east Asia has prompted Washington to blacklist some companies in the region, with Malaysia pledging to tell data centre operators not to host, lease space or provide services to the firms.

The country is considering replacing some of its coal fleet with nuclear power to meet the growing demand, although that isn’t slated to happen until 2040.

Malaysia announced plans this month to launch a separate wholesale electricity market for large power consumers including data centres, to safeguard supply for households and factories. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Consumer protection panel proposes cooling-off period for prepaid packages, higher cap on small claims
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Consumers could have a mandated period to reconsider their expensive prepaid packages and cancel without penalty if recommendations by a panel are taken up by the Government.

The panel, which was tasked to review Singapore’s consumer protection regime, said consumers who may have come under undue sales pressure should have a window to reconsider after leaving the shop. It suggested rolling this out in high-risk sectors, naming the beauty and wellness sector as a priority.

Announcing its proposals on Nov 27, the panel also recommended more influencer advertisement transparency and stronger ticketing protection. It submitted its seven recommendations to the Government on the same day.

This is the first comprehensive review of Singapore’s consumer protection regime since the last major amendment to the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act in 2018, said the panel’s co-chair Melvin Yong, who is president of the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE).

Should the recommendations be approved, more consumers could also take their disputes to court.

The panel suggested that the Small Claims Tribunal (SCT) increase its standard limit for consumer claims to S$30,000, up from S$20,000 currently. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Asean equities in for a ride in 2027; Singapore, Vietnam favoured: JPMorgan
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore and Vietnam are the two Asean equity markets JPMorgan Chase analysts are “overweight” on, even while the region is expected to face headwinds in the first half of 2027.

This comes as economists expect three more rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve – in January and March 2027, on top of December this year.

US dollar strength will rise with the move, and “pressure” emerging market currencies too, noted a Thursday (Nov 26) report.

“Almost all Asean central banks would deliver rate hikes over the next few months to stymie inflation and defend their currencies,” said the analysts.

“This is done in an environment where the fiscal budgets have limited room for growth support...(such that) earnings growth might remain under pressure.”

For Singapore equities, the JPMorgan analysts stand by their earnings quality and dividend visibility, especially with substantial “fiscal support” on top of the ongoing Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP), which is expected to boost market liquidity in early 2027.

Launched in February 2025, the EQDP is Singapore’s S$6.5 billion equity market stimulus programme, with S$5.4 billion allocated to three groups of fund managers so far. A fourth tranche of fund managers will be appointed in 2027.

Others are less bullish on the city-state’s equity market moving into 2027, however. Citi analysts earlier put an “underweight” rating on the Singapore market relative to others in the Asean region.

Morgan Stanley analysts also said there is an “incremental negative from an investor risk perception” for Singapore, along with Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, after news of fresh tariffs and a freeze on Nvidia chip shipments to the four countries, a Friday report by The Business Times indicated.

They noted, however, that Singapore’s growth outlook is unlikely to be affected by this.

Economists have kept their non-oil domestic export (NODX) 2027 forecasts for the country unchanged, with some noting how the impact should be “relatively contained”.

Meanwhile, Vietnam was also upgraded to “overweight” by the JPMorgan analysts, from a “neutral” rating previously, due to monetary easing after a tightening phase.

“Corporate earnings would be underpinned by a ramp-up in public infrastructure investment and strong economic momentum,” they wrote.

Vietnam’s most recent structural reforms, “Doi Moi 2.0”, began in late 2024 and include construction of the country’s new International Financial Centre, and various transport and energy partnerships.

A year of two halves

Although JPMorgan forecasts a volatile H1 2027, it expects improvement in H2.

“Silver linings” could appear in the second half, especially when the need to diversify from artificial intelligence plays picks up, as market sentiment becomes more selective in 2027.

Fluctuating energy prices could be a catalyst, too.

“While the Middle-East situation outlook remains limited, alternative supply and sustained reduction in oil demand is bringing the oil market back to a surplus and points to lower oil prices in 2027,” the analysts wrote.

Such circumstances will offer significant support to Asean’s current account flows and ease inflationary pressures “materially”, they added.

Brent oil prices are set to decline to US$55 per barrel by end-2027, according to JPMorgan’s commodities team.

data.title: China’s industrial profit growth fastest in five months as recovery remains uneven
data.description:
[BEIJING] Profit growth at China’s industrial firms accelerated in October to the fastest in five months, supported by improving conditions in parts of the manufacturing sector, although broader economic momentum remained subdued.

The industrial profits data are closely watched as a gauge of corporate health, investment appetite and the effectiveness of Beijing’s stimulus measures. The figures also offer clues on whether stronger earnings could reduce pressure for further policy easing.

Profits at industrial firms rose 20.1 per cent from a year earlier last month, versus a 14.4 per cent gain in September, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Friday (Nov 27).

Profits were up 16 per cent in the first 10 months, accelerating from a 15.5 per cent increase in the January-September period.

But the breakdown highlighted a widening divergence across sectors.

Profit growth in AI-related industries and upstream sectors is outpacing that of downstream industries, while external demand remains an important source of support, said Ding Meng, Citic Bank International’s chief China economist.

The bureau’s data showed that profits in computer, telecommunications and other electronic equipment manufacturing doubled in the first 10 months, while furniture manufacturing posted a decline of 52.4 per cent.

“The recovery remains uneven and provides a more mixed signal on the health of the broader economy,” said Lynn Song, ING’s Greater China chief economist.

Broader Chinese indices were muted while tech stocks rebounded strongly. The CSI Semiconductor Industry Index jumped more than 5 per cent, while the Hang Seng Tech Index was up 3 per cent.

The disparity underscores the challenges facing policymakers as domestic demand remains weak and continues to weigh on large parts of the corporate sector.

Many manufacturers have increasingly relied on overseas sales to sustain growth, leaving them exposed to rising trade frictions and geopolitical risks.

Beijing has rolled out a series of support measures in recent months, including interest-rate cuts, liquidity injections and targeted financing support for sectors such as technology, manufacturing and infrastructure.

Still, analysts say the impact has been mixed, with weak household demand and lingering strains in the property sector continuing to drag on the broader recovery.

“The robust pace of profit growth further reinforces expectations that there will be no additional monetary policy easing in the near term,” Ding said.

The outlook for exports, a key source of support for manufacturers this year, has also become less certain. Concern over potential tariff increases and other trade restrictions, particularly in the United States and the European Union, has raised questions about the sustainability of export-driven growth.

Looking ahead, a potential slowdown in AI data centre investment, concerns over AI-sector profitability and leverage, and the risk of further Western restrictions on Chinese exports mean that “boosting domestic demand as soon as possible remains the key to sustaining profit growth,” Ding said.

Industrial profit figures cover firms with annual revenue of at least 20 million yuan (US$3 million) from main operations. BLOOMBERG

data.title: JPMorgan, BlackRock, Endowus frontrunners in scheme to lift returns on S$700 billion of CPF savings
data.description:
JPMORGAN Asset Management, BlackRock and Endowus Singapore are the frontrunners to manage a slice of Singapore’s S$701 billion (US$543 billion) public pension fund.

The three firms submitted proposals to run a new investment programme that offers an alternative for members of the Central Provident Fund who want to earn more than the government-guaranteed return, according to people familiar with the matter.

The winners will be announced in the first half of 2027. Discussions are preliminary and no final decisions have been made, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

JPMorgan would partner with Singapore’s largest bank, DBS, in an extension of a retirement portfolio programme that was piloted in 2024. Endowus, an investment platform, is in talks to work with Capital Group on the CPF programme, said the people.

A spokesperson for the CPF Board said the evaluation process is ongoing, and it can’t comment on individual applications.

JPMorgan and Capital Group declined to comment. Endowus said it has been a digital adviser for investing CPF savings since 2019. BlackRock and DBS didn’t respond to requests for comment.

The investment plan was unveiled by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in this year’s budget speech as a way to deal with the country’s aging population, and will be launched in 2028.

The new programme will allow members to opt in to portfolio strategies that automatically adjust according to their age. As investors get older, the equity allocation will shift to lower-risk assets such as bonds, before being liquidated in phases by a set target date.

Currently, members have the option of manually picking investments, including bonds, stocks and unit trusts, from a list of more than 30 asset managers. As of September, just S$22 billion – or 3 per cent – of net assets were invested in this optional plan, according to the CPF website.

The bulk of CPF savings are invested by the pension board in Special Singapore Government Securities. Proceeds from these securities are pooled with other government funds, including from budget surpluses and land sales, and managed by sovereign wealth fund GIC for long-term returns. Members under 55 earn risk-free interest of up to 5 per cent a year.

Founded in 1955, the CPF is Singapore’s mandatory pension fund for citizens and permanent residents to support retirement, housing and health-care needs. There are more than two million active members, and over S$14 billion in CPF contributions were received in the third quarter. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Asean must counter economic nationalism with deeper integration, wider partnerships: DPM Gan
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Asean must counter rising economic nationalism with deeper integration and wider partnerships, in a world where governments are placing more emphasis on self-reliance and control over critical industries, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Nov 27.

“Raising barriers among ourselves would narrow the opportunities available to each of us,” he said. A more integrated Asean would strengthen its value as a partner, while broader tie-ups open up more opportunities for the region.

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), was delivering a keynote speech at SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit 2026, jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

The annual event gathered policymakers, business leaders and industry experts, with OCBC as the presenting sponsor, Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

In his speech, Gan identified three factors that make integration and partnerships especially important: artificial intelligence, geopolitical shocks and geo-economic contestation. “Each can strengthen the impulse to turn inward. Yet each also makes cooperation more crucial,” he said.

His remarks followed the United States’ announcements of fresh tariffs and chip export restrictions over the past two weeks, moves which affected many in South-east Asia as the region finds itself in the crosshairs of sharpening rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

“Geo-economic competition is reshaping the networks through which we trade, invest and access technology,” Gan said, with governments paying closer attention to dependencies and control over critical capabilities.

“Asean countries cannot determine how major powers manage their differences,” he added. “But we can maintain relationships across these divides and remain a bridge for trade, investment and cooperation.”

Doing so would require that Asean earn and sustain its partners’ confidence in the grouping’s integrity, institutional reliability and business environment by issuing clear and predictable rules, upholding its laws and commitments, and taking firm action against wrongdoing, he said.

“As scrutiny of international trade and investment intensifies, maintaining these standards becomes even more important,” he added.

ASEAN will mark its 60th anniversary in 2027, with Singapore pushing for deeper integration and wider partnerships as it takes on Asean’s rotating chairmanship at a time of heightened geopolitical contestation.

Both the US and China would continue to be key economic partners for Asean, Gan said, with their businesses, technologies and markets important to the region’s growth.

Both countries are among the region’s largest trading partners and sources of foreign direct investment.

In tandem, the grouping is strengthening tie-ups with other partners that would expand the region’s economic options and reduce its exposure to disruptions, Gan said.

These include negotiations to upgrade Asean’s trade agreements with South Korea and Canada, moves to expand and enhance the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and growing links with other regional groupings such as the European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Asean is also strengthening integration within the grouping, with Gan highlighting recent efforts that would help firms better tap suppliers and customers within the region.

A recently upgraded Asean Trade in Goods Agreement, set to be rolled out in end-2026, will help businesses reduce costs through streamlined procedures and more transparent rules, he said, while a customs-related mutual recognition arrangement would give trusted traders faster clearances and priority treatment in participating countries.

And a regional Digital Economy Framework Agreement signed earlier in the month would make cross-border transactions, payments and access to digital services easier, he added.

These would make Asean more valuable as a place to produce and market to serve, and form a stronger regional base enabling the grouping to “engage the world with greater confidence”, Gan said. THE STRAITS TIMES

  • For more information, visit www.asiafuturesummit.com

JPMORGAN Asset Management, BlackRock and Endowus Singapore are the frontrunners to manage a slice of Singapore’s S$701 billion (US$543 billion) public pension fund.

The three firms submitted proposals to run a new investment programme that offers an alternative for members of the Central Provident Fund who want to earn more than the government-guaranteed return, according to people familiar with the matter.

The winners will be announced in the first half of 2027. Discussions are preliminary and no final decisions have been made, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

JPMorgan would partner with Singapore’s largest bank, DBS, in an extension of a retirement portfolio programme that was piloted in 2024. Endowus, an investment platform, is in talks to work with Capital Group on the CPF programme, said the people.

A spokesperson for the CPF Board said the evaluation process is ongoing, and it can’t comment on individual applications.

JPMorgan and Capital Group declined to comment. Endowus said it has been a digital adviser for investing CPF savings since 2019. BlackRock and DBS didn’t respond to requests for comment.

The investment plan was unveiled by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in this year’s budget speech as a way to deal with the country’s aging population, and will be launched in 2028.

The new programme will allow members to opt in to portfolio strategies that automatically adjust according to their age. As investors get older, the equity allocation will shift to lower-risk assets such as bonds, before being liquidated in phases by a set target date.

Currently, members have the option of manually picking investments, including bonds, stocks and unit trusts, from a list of more than 30 asset managers. As of September, just S$22 billion – or 3 per cent – of net assets were invested in this optional plan, according to the CPF website.

The bulk of CPF savings are invested by the pension board in Special Singapore Government Securities. Proceeds from these securities are pooled with other government funds, including from budget surpluses and land sales, and managed by sovereign wealth fund GIC for long-term returns. Members under 55 earn risk-free interest of up to 5 per cent a year.

Founded in 1955, the CPF is Singapore’s mandatory pension fund for citizens and permanent residents to support retirement, housing and health-care needs. There are more than two million active members, and over S$14 billion in CPF contributions were received in the third quarter. BLOOMBERG
